claims.text: Coherent or semi-coherent interfaces between distinct HEA coating layers pin dislocations.
Secondary precipitates, such as a thin HCP phase at layer interfaces, further hinder dislocation motion.
Interface pinning and secondary precipitation reduce time-dependent plastic deformation in multilayer HEA coatings.
The proposed multilayer coating has repeated layers of comparable overall composition but distinct phase distributions.
The proposed layer boundaries can host nanoscale secondary precipitates of an HCP-type phase.
Layer interfaces provide energy barriers to dislocation glide.
Layer interfaces provide energy barriers to dislocation climb.
Interfacial HCP precipitation impedes dislocation motion through conventional precipitation hardening.
HCP-phase formation under HIP in a related refractory HEA was accompanied by increased microhardness.
High-temperature sustained mechanical loading can be used to induce and measure creep deformation.
The proposed comparison is conducted at approximately 500–700°C under constant load.
Multilayer HEA coatings will have lower creep rates than homogeneous single-layer coatings of the same overall composition and thickness.
Multilayer HEA coatings will retain more microhardness than homogeneous single-layer coatings during high-temperature loading.
Multilayer HEA coatings will accumulate less plastic strain over time than homogeneous single-layer coatings.
The mechanism is expected to dominate when layer thickness preserves interface integrity.
The mechanism applies only at temperatures where interdiffusion or loss of interface coherency does not occur.
Interfacial decohesion or brittle fracture at extreme temperatures or stresses can place the coating outside the proposed mechanism's applicable regime.

A failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-rate reduction together with no superior hardness retention and no evidence of interface-driven dislocation pinning would falsify the proposed mechanism.
